ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Howard Hughes Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care ten months after a plane crash: contamination fears with washing and avoidance, chronic pain on long-term codeine, an opioid review, hearing, weight, kidney health and safety. Concerns: He wants to get back to full days of work without hours of washing and checking, and without other people seeing his rituals; He is afraid that without codeine the pain from the crash will stop him working; He wants his privacy protected and nothing about his care known outside the clinic. [S]

Naloxone 4 mg nasal spray, one spray into one nostril for a suspected opioid overdose, repeated every two to three minutes in the other nostril if needed; two-pack dispensed, with instruction for him and his household staff

list.item: Aviator, aircraft builder and film producer who owns and runs several companies; test-flies his own aircraft; working long irregular hours on a very large flying boat [S]
Unmarried; lives alone in a rented house with a household staff of several employees and a personal assistant; no relative is involved in his care or named in this record [S]

His staff follow written rules he has set: they wash their hands before handing him anything, pass him objects wrapped in tissue, prepare his food in a set way, and keep visitors away; he can pay for every ritual to be carried out for him [S]

Codeine: acetaminophen-codeine tablets since the crash, now 10 to 12 a day from two prescribers at two pharmacies; no other opioids, no injection, no drugs from any other source. Alcohol: rarely (AUDIT-C 1). Never smoked tobacco [S]
Eats one meal a day that he has watched being prepared, plus milk from sealed bottles; skips meals when he cannot inspect the food [S]
No firearms in the home; drives himself and still flies [S]
Strengths: engineering talent, persistence, courage as a pilot, the resources to pay for care, loyal staff, and his own wish to get back to work without the rituals [S]

tr.td: Establishing primary care ten months after a plane crash: contamination fears with washing and avoidance, chronic pain on long-term codeine, an opioid review, hearing, weight, kidney health and safety
One-week review, seen the same day by psychiatry: the diagnosis of OCD, an SSRI, exposure and response prevention, and starting buprenorphine
Five-week review: OCD treatment, buprenorphine, pain, the audiogram and weight
Ten-week review: sertraline to an OCD dose, exposure therapy and his staff's part in it, hearing aids and pain
Twenty-two-week review: response of OCD, buprenorphine maintenance, pain, weight and laboratory checks
Same-day sick visit for a cough

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, advise on an SSRI at OCD doses with buprenorphine, plan exposure and response prevention, and advise on how his staff can stop carrying out rituals for him

Opioid review under the CDC 2022 guideline: benefits and harms reviewed with him, a prescription drug monitoring program check before every controlled-substance prescription, urine drug testing with consent and explained as part of care, one prescriber and one pharmacy, a nonjudgmental DSM-5-TR assessment for opioid use disorder, and no abrupt stop of codeine

Buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid use disorder and pain: induction in the clinic at one week after about 20 hours without codeine, then 8 mg twice daily, dispensed weekly at first; naloxone nasal spray at home; no benzodiazepines; leftover codeine to a pharmacy take-back

Pain after major trauma: scheduled acetaminophen up to 3,000 mg a day, physical therapy for the chest wall, left shoulder and low back, graded activity, sleep, and pain coping skills woven into his therapy; no NSAID long term

OCD treatment: exposure and response prevention with a psychologist, weekly 90-minute sessions with home practice, then twice weekly; sertraline from 50 mg, raised every four to six weeks as tolerated toward 200 mg; response judged by the Y-BOCS at each visit; augmentation with a low-dose antipsychotic (aripiprazole or risperidone) or a switch to clomipramine considered only if the response is poor after 8 to 12 weeks at the highest tolerated dose

Accommodation by staff: with his written consent, his assistant joins two therapy sessions; staff stop carrying out rituals for him in planned steps that follow his exposure hierarchy, offer support instead of reassurance, and are not asked to report on him
Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone, means safety for opioids, and safety review at every visit
Hearing: audiometry, then hearing aids and a remote microphone if hearing loss is confirmed; hearing protection when flying and in the factory

Nutrition and weight: a dietitian visit, three meals a day built into his exposure plan (food made by his cook, then food from a restaurant), weight at each visit, albumin at baseline and follow-up; no supplements needed

Kidney health: creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin at baseline and a metabolic panel at follow-up while on scheduled acetaminophen and any new medicine; acetaminophen kept at or below 3,000 mg a day; no long-term NSAID
Privacy: care documented in the clinic record only; letters about his health go only to people he names
Y-BOCS down by at least 35 percent (response) within six months
Y-BOCS 28 at intake, 14 at twenty-two weeks (a 50 percent fall); washing and checking about one hour a day
Stop codeine and stay on buprenorphine with no use of other opioids
Codeine stopped at one week; all urine tests positive for buprenorphine and negative for other opioids
Pain that lets him work and sleep: PEG at or below 4
PEG 6.7 at intake to 4.0 at twenty-two weeks
Regain weight to at least 76 kg with regular meals
72.0 kg at intake to 76.2 kg; three meals a day, including food prepared by his cook
Follow conversation in meetings with hearing aids
Hearing aids fitted at ten weeks and worn every day
Staff stop carrying out rituals for him, step by step, by his own plan
Tissue-wrapping and the hand-washing rule for staff stopped; food preparation rules relaxed; visitors no longer screened for illness

list.item: Independent in all activities; spends about four hours a day on washing and checking; avoids meetings and handshakes; reaches overhead with the left arm only with pain [S]

Alert, intense and courteous; declines to shake hands and keeps his gloves on until he has washed; speech normal in rate, a little loud; mood anxious; contamination obsessions with washing, cleaning and avoidance compulsions, Y-BOCS 28 (obsessions 14, compulsions 14); he says the fears are probably excessive (good or fair insight); no hallucinations or delusions; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 2026-05-04: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with weekly visits at first. Risk factors reviewed without detail: a breakdown in earlier years, opioid use disorder, chronic pain, severe OCD, isolation and anxiety. No current thoughts of suicide. Opioids are dangerous in overdose, so means safety is part of the plan: naloxone nasal spray at home with his staff taught to use it, unused codeine tablets taken to a pharmacy take-back, and buprenorphine dispensed one week at a time at first. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit [S]
